newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana seeks strategic investors for three banks.
newsitem.headline: Ghana seeks strategic investors for three banks.

text.p: Ghana is looking for investors to take up strategic stakes of about 30 percent each in three state-controlled banks, a senior government official said.

"We have reserved stakes of about 30 percent in each of the three banks for strategic investors," said Mercy Mamle Tetteh, chief manager of the government's Financial Sector Adjustment Programme (FINSAP).
"But this percentage is negotiable; it can be more or less, depending on what the investor has to offer," she told Reuters.
The banks are Social Security Bank Ltd (SSB), Ghana Commercial Bank Ltd (GCB) and National Investment Bank Ltd (NIB).

A FINSAP document describes a strategic investor as one who brings "additional strength to the divested banks through broader market linkages, improvement in systems, better product engineering, strong management as may be required, and of course, additional equity."

The goverment owns 58 percent of GCB, Ghana's leading commercial bank, with the public holding the remaining 42 percent. The bank made net earnings of 42.6 billion cedis in 1995, against 33.3 billion in 1994.
Its assets of 568.1 billion cedis represent 29 percent of the total for Ghana's banking industry, GCB officials said.
A public share offer by GCB in March this year was oversubscribed by 38 percent.

SSB is largely owned by the quasi-government Social Security and National Insurance Trust (SSNIT), which holds a 73.61 percent stake. Public shareholders own 21.09 percent while the government directly holds a 5.30 percent slice. The 30 percent stake to be divested will come from the SSNIT holding.
This year SSB, one of Ghana's largest four banks, made a first-half net profit of 11.1 billion cedis against 5.8 billion cedis for the first half of 1995.

However, an SSB public share offer in mid-1995 was undersubscribed by 30 percent. Analysts blamed this on bad timing -- shortly after floods in Accra forced institutional investors to channel cash to settling claims.
The government holds 87.6 percent of shares in NIB, with the the rest held by about 4,000 small shareholders. The 30 percent to be sold to a core investor will come from the state's share.

Since concluding a restructuring programme five years ago, NIB's net profit jumped from 665 million cedis in 1991 to 7.18 billion cedis in 1995, according FINSAP figures. The net profit for 1994 was 6.2 billion cedis.
For NIB a strategic investor is being sought before a private placement and/or a public share offering to dispose of any remaining shares.

"For NIB four groups have put in bid so far. They include banks and overseas investment firms," FINSAP's Tetteh said. "The bidding is still open. Afterwards we will decide whether there is need for a public flotation of shares."
